concept.title: Tables
concept.abstract: This section covers the Table style in Markdown — the primary structure for presenting information with inherent row-and-column relationships — and ten scenarios: a standard multi-column table, a table with a caption, a table with no header row, merged cells, nested tables, lists and images inside table cells, tables spanning multiple pages, consecutive tables, and a two-column parameter table in a reference topic. The converter reads each table's structure, cell complexity, and topic context to determine whether to map it to <simpletable>, a CALS <table>, or <properties>.

section.p: ATable is the primary structure for reference and lookup content. It is a structural mechanism to present information that has inherent row-and-column relationships — parameter names and their values, feature names and their states, error codes and their meanings, API fields and their data types.

A table reduces a lookup task from reading a paragraph to scanning a row and column. In DITA-XML, a table is structured data — each cell is a discrete, addressable unit that a transform can reformat for PDF, or online help output, filter by column for conditional publishing, and extract independently for reuse in other deliverables.Standard Markdown tables do not support block-level elements such as lists inside table cells. Because each table row must be represented on a single line, lists and other complex content cannot be interpreted as part of the table structure during conversion.

Markdown tables use pipe (|) syntax to represent structured information. Readers recognize tables as rows and columns that organize related data into an easy-to-scan format. During conversion, the table structure and the surrounding content help determine how the information should be represented in DITA. Different table structures may represent simple reference data, parameter definitions, configuration settings, or other specialized information.Standard Markdown tables support only simple row-and-column structures created using pipe (|) syntax. They do not support merged rows, merged columns, or nested tables. These structures can only be created using embedded HTML, which is not converted by the Markdown-to-DITA converter.

The converter analyzes each Markdown table together with its surrounding context to determine the most appropriate DITA table structure. Depending on the complexity of the table and the information it contains, the converter generates either a DITA <simpletable>, a CALS <table>, or a specialized <properties> element. Table content, including supported embedded images and empty cells, is preserved during conversion.Author tables using standard Markdown pipe syntax. Tables created as screenshots or other non-tabular content cannot be interpreted as structured tables and are converted according to their content type rather than as DITA tables.
The following sections demonstrate how different Markdown table structures are interpreted during Markdown-to-DITA conversion and how they affect the generated DITA output.
